items.title: Mass protests that led to regime change had their heyday between 1980 and 2011: what happened?
items.summary: People are taking to the streets across the world. In 2025, mass mobilisation occurred in countries such as Morocco , Tanzania and Turkey . In Madagascar , protests resulted in president Andry Rajoelina fleeing the country in October. More recently, protesters have filled the streets from France and Italy to Senegal and Kenya. By mass mobilisation , we mean sustained, organised campaigns of protests that involve more than 1,000 people, aimed at changing a country’s political regime or removing the government or leader. Mass mobilisation has historically been seen as a viable path to democracy. Ferdinand Marcos left Manila in 1986 after weeks of popular protests. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 after months of demonstrations in East Germany. South Africa’s apartheid regime yielded to domestic and international pressure in the 1990s. The examples are many, and mass movements have been a driving force to democratic change in authoritarian regimes. Yet the historical record is less clear-cut. items.title: Scientists find way to repair heart damage after a heart attack
items.summary: Every year, millions of people worldwide suffer a heart attack. Thanks to advances in emergency treatment, many now survive an event that might once have been fatal. Yet surviving a heart attack is not necessarily the end of the story. The damage can be permanent, increasing the risk of heart failure, breathlessness and a poorer quality of life. Researchers have developed an experimental treatment that could change how we approach recovery after a heart attack . Rather than simply protecting the remaining heart muscle, the new approach aims to encourage the heart to repair itself. So far, it has only been tested in mice. The findings, published in the journal Nature Cardiovascular Research , describe how modified messenger RNA (mRNA) can encourage heart muscle cells to multiply, potentially improving the heart’s ability to pump blood. Although this is still early-stage research, the study offers the tantalising possibility that one day we might be able to encourage the adult human heart to regenerate damaged muscle. items.title: NEET UG 2026 paper leak: Fast track court frames charges against 14 accused
items.summary: A Delhi court on Wednesday ordered the framing of criminal charges against 14 persons accused in the NEET UG 2026 paper leak case. Special Judge Ajay Gupta of the fast-track court at Rouse Avenue Court framed charges against them under the Bharatiya Nagarik Sanhita, the Prevention of Corruption Act, and the Public Examination Prevention of Unfair Means Act. Accused Yash Yadav, Mangilal Biwal, Dinesh Biwal, Vikas Biwal, Shubham Khairnar, Dhananjay Lokhande, Prahlad Kulkarni, Tejas Harshad Kumar, Dr Manoj Shirure, Shivraj Raghunath Motegaonkar, Manisha Waghmare, Manisha Mandhare, Manisha Sanjay Havaldar and Sheshrao Bajrang Suryavanshi have been charged with the offences. Notably, the Court said that it will start the day-to-day trial in the case from November 25. The CBI has filed a nearly 20,000-page chargesheet in the NEET UG paper leak case. It names 14 persons as accused. In the chargesheet, the agency had stated that 3 subject experts leaked the NEET exam questions from the National Testing Agency (NTA) office in Delhi through different methods. The Court had been told that the accused were able to do it because they were not frisked while exiting the confidential section.
